name: Hassan Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Hassan, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign for anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. This is a made-up study built around people like you, and there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at seven for an early lecture in thermodynamics, then statics and a CAD workshop where we model brackets and gears on the computer. I pray at the prayer room in the student centre at lunch with a few other guys, and afterwards we eat in the canteen and argue about football. Weekends I go home on the coach, about two hours, to help at my father's shop. We sell car parts and tyres, and I do the stock counts on Saturdays.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I grew up in the shop, so I like engines and how things fit together. My father said do a degree first and then decide if you want the shop. I had top results, and my parents pay my fees and my room, so no debt. I use an AI assistant sometimes, for example when a CAD error makes no sense, but I don't trust it with anything that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, nothing to see. It helps a little with emails and some parts catalogues, and that's all. I'd tell my friends that hard work and a good trade still matter more than whatever's in the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calm. My degree is useful, the shop is steady, and my family isn't depending on anything unusual. I'd keep thinking about the shop's future, since online sellers have been taking customers for years, but that's an old problem and not an AI one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my degree and look for a summer internship at a car or machinery maker. I'd keep helping at the shop on Saturdays, and I'd suggest to my father that we put the stock list on a simple app so he could check it from home. I'd keep my prayers and my routine, because it keeps me steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels settled. A bit like a good meal where nothing's too spicy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned online sellers. Is the shop under pressure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. People look up the part on their phone and buy it from a big website. My father says the ones who stay are the ones who need advice or a quick fix. My father would tell you the shop has survived worse, and that trust is the product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to run the shop one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, in a few years, after I've worked somewhere else. I'd like to know what a big company does before I do it my way. My father says he won't push me, but I can see he'd like the shop to stay in the family.

say: I'd say there's **nothing** to see, since hard work and a good trade matter more than the news.
I'd tell friends AI helps with **emails** and little else.
think: I'd feel **calm**: the degree is useful and the shop is steady.
Online sellers are an **old** problem, not an AI one.
do: Look for a summer **internship** at a car or machinery maker.
Suggest my father put the stock list on a simple **app**.
feel: **Settled**, like a good meal where nothing is too spicy.
S0.quote: My father would tell you the shop has survived worse, and that trust is the product.
fieldNote: Calm because both the degree and the family **shop** feel steady.
Sees online sellers as the shop's real pressure, a point he separates from AI.
Wants to work elsewhere before deciding about the shop, a mark of steady adaptability.

steps.text: Apply for a summer internship at a machinery or car maker
Put the shop's stock list on a simple phone app
Keep helping at the shop on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change we can handle if people keep their feet on the ground. I'd say routine jobs, like copying data and answering the same questions, will go to software, and hands-on skills will be worth more. I'd say that to my friends and to my father's customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more serious. My course has a lot of design work and calculations on a computer, and that's the thinking work the card names. But the shop is hands-on, the mechanical side is slow to change, and I'd feel like I'm on the safer side of the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my degree and push towards the practical modules: machine design, manufacturing and materials. I'd use the AI tools for CAD checks and report drafts, since everyone else will. I'd also help my father put the shop's ordering and invoicing on software, so he spends less time on paperwork and more on customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a busy road at rush hour. You can't stop it, but you can stay in your lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first change you'd see in your father's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Customers asking questions to a chatbot first, then arriving with an answer that's half right. And supplier websites ordering parts automatically. My father would be annoyed at first, then he'd use it, because he's practical like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell classmates who ignore the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them a calculator never replaced an engineer, but an engineer who refuses a calculator is slow. I'd show them how I check the assistant's output, and say don't copy anything you can't explain.

say: I'd say routine jobs go to software and **hands-on** skills become worth more.
I'd say it is a change we can **handle** with feet on the ground.
think: I'd feel more **serious**, since my design and calculation work is thinking work.
The shop is hands-on, so I'm on the **safer** side of the line.
do: Push towards **practical** modules: machine design, manufacturing and materials.
Use AI for CAD **checks** and report drafts.
Move the shop's **ordering** and invoicing onto software.
feel: Like a busy road at rush hour: stay in your **lane**.
S1.quote: A calculator never replaced an engineer, but an engineer who refuses a calculator is slow.
fieldNote: Uses a **line** between thinking work and hands-on work to place himself and the shop.
Practical about tools: he'd use AI because rivals will, with checks.
Mood is uneasy: his own job looks safe, but the shop's customers and ordering are shifting.

steps.text: Take machine design and manufacturing modules next term
Use AI to check CAD models and draft lab reports
Move the shop's ordering and invoicing onto simple software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and I'd say it plainly: families and shops need time. I'd say we should stand together, help each other and lean on our communities, and I'd say governments should not make it worse with rules that slow small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious. Within two years the thinking jobs I'm studying for could go, and my degree would be only half done. My father's shop is hands-on, so it has until about 2031, but the ordering, the website and the customers' questions would change straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my degree but learn a trade next to it. My father could teach me some mechanical repair properly, and I'd get a licence if there's one. I'd cut my own spending and put away everything I earn. I'd also talk to my uncle about what the family would do together if the shop had to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long drive at night on a road I don't know. I'd hold onto the wheel and pray a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk about it with your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Respectfully. He'd say don't worry, which is what he says every time. I'd say, Baba, let's make a list of what we'd cut and what we'd keep. He'd listen if I put it as planning and not as fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the shop's income dropped by half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut hours before we cut people, and we'd sell what we don't need. I'd work extra weekends. I'd not ask my parents for more help, but I'd accept it if they offered, because family does that.

say: I'd say it's too fast and families and shops need **time**.
I'd say communities should stand **together** and not rely on slow rules.
think: I'd be **anxious**: my degree would be half done when thinking jobs go.
My father's shop has until about **2031**, but ordering and customer questions change at once.
do: Stay in the degree and learn **mechanical repair** from my father.
Cut my **spending** and put away everything I earn.
Talk to my **uncle** about what the family would do together.
feel: Like a long drive at **night** on an unknown road, praying a lot.
S2.quote: I'd say, Baba, let's make a list of what we'd cut and what we'd keep.
fieldNote: He treats fear as a **planning** problem he can raise respectfully with his father.
Turns to family, community and prayer before government.
Anxious but with control: family savings and a trade fallback keep him from alarmed.

steps.text: Learn mechanical repair properly from his father
Put away everything earned from weekend work
Cut his own spending on extras
Plan with his uncle how the family would cope

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is some warning, so let's be sensible. I'd say people should learn skills that last and keep their savings in order. I'd say governments should help with training, and not make it a political fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but not afraid. I'd graduate in three years and I'd be competing with software for the entry-level roles. But hands-on work stays until around 2034, and I'd have time to get practical experience in a factory or workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with machine design and manufacturing, and do placements in a real plant. I'd work at my father's shop through summers and take over the stock system with software. I'd save part of my pay and keep expenses low. I'd start to use AI tools more once I'm sure about the good ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the weather forecast says rain in a few days. You find your umbrella and carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having five years change your plan with the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me think of the shop as a real option, not an emergency. I could finish the degree, work a few years elsewhere, and come back with systems that make it work for the next twenty years. In two years I'd be hurrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take the shop over earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my father's health dropped or if companies stopped hiring junior engineers. Then it makes sense for me to be there and keep the income in the family. I'd not like to, but I'd do it.

say: I'd say five years is some **warning**, so learn lasting skills and keep savings in order.
I'd say governments should help with **training** without a political fight.
think: I'd be **uneasy** but not afraid, competing with software for entry-level roles.
Hands-on work stays until around 2034, so I'd have time for **practical** experience.
do: Finish the degree with machine design and **manufacturing**, plus plant placements.
Work at the **shop** each summer and set up its stock system.
Save part of my **pay** and keep expenses low.
feel: Like a forecast of **rain** in a few days: find your umbrella and carry on.
S3.quote: Five years lets me think of the shop as a real option, not an emergency.
fieldNote: Time turns the shop from an **emergency** into a real option; he states the difference himself.
Sets conditions for taking over earlier: his father's health or graduate hiring drying up.
Uneasy because he'd graduate into a changing job market.

steps.text: Do a placement at a manufacturing plant next summer
Set up the shop's stock system on software in summers
Save part of every pay and keep expenses low

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough that nobody should panic. I'd say we should look after each other, teach young people real skills, and not trust anyone who claims to know the exact date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be calm. Ten years takes me through the degree and a few years of work, and I'd have time to decide about the shop with a clear head. My father would be near sixty, and he could choose when to step back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on: finish the degree, work for a manufacturer for a few years, and keep helping at the shop. I'd save a deposit for a home. I'd learn to use AI tools well, because they'd be standard by then, and I'd help my father make the shop easier to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels peaceful. I'd think of it as one of the many things my family has had to adjust to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan differently for your own family in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd not delay marrying and having children out of fear, and I'd think about it on a normal timeline. Ten years gives time for that. I'd just want to have a stable job, a home and a good family around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first sign that ten years was too long a window?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the machinery maker I worked for started using robots for tasks my team does, or if my father's suppliers moved everything to automatic ordering. I'd treat those as signs to bring forward plans.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough that nobody should **panic**.
I'd say don't trust anyone who claims to know the exact **date**.
think: I'd be **calm**, with time to decide about the shop with a clear head.
My father could choose when to **step back**.
do: Finish the degree and work for a **manufacturer** for a few years.
Learn AI tools **well** and help the shop run more easily.
feel: **Peaceful**, one of many things my family has had to adjust to.
S4.quote: I'd not delay marrying and having children out of fear
fieldNote: The decade lets him plan **family** life normally, which he stresses.
Names signs to watch: robots in his team's tasks and automatic ordering at the shop's suppliers.
Calm follows from time, a stable degree and a father who can pace his own retirement.

steps.text: Work a few years at a manufacturer after graduating
Save a deposit for a home
Help his father make the shop easier to run

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It leaves no space for families to talk and plan. What would help is time to train, honest information about which jobs will stay, and communities that look after their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against change. I use the tools when they're proven. I just want young people to be told the truth and given real skills, not slogans.

headlineQuote: I just want young people to be told the truth and given real skills, not slogans.
portrait: Hassan is an 18-year-old **mechanical engineering** student whose father runs a car-parts and tyre shop.
He is traditional and steady: he prays, trusts family and community, and uses AI sometimes but checks it.
He sees a line between **thinking work** and hands-on work, and puts himself and the shop on the safer side.
His fallbacks are the shop, a trade skill and savings, and he treats fear as something to plan.
He stays calm or uneasy in most pictures and turns **anxious** in the two-year picture.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because it leaves no space for families to talk and plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Time to train**, honest information on which jobs stay, and communities that look after their own.
